related_questions.question: How to stop arthritis from getting worse?
related_questions.snippet: As long as you do the right type and level of exercise for your condition, your arthritis won't get any worse. Combined with a healthy, balanced diet, regular exercise will help you lose weight and place less strain on your joints. Your GP can recommend the type and level of exercise that's right for you.

text_blocks.snippet: Arthritis can start at any age, but generally, osteoarthritis (OA) is more common in people over 50, while rheumatoid arthritis (RA) typically develops between ages 30 and 50. related_questions.snippet: Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs) NSAIDs relieve pain and inflammation by blocking hormone-like substances called prostaglandins. Naproxen (Aleve), aspirin and ibuprofen (Motrin, Advil) are available over the counter. Others like indomethacin (Indocin) and celecoxib (Celebrex) require a prescription.

related_questions.question: Is arthritis painful all the time?
related_questions.snippet: The main symptoms of osteoarthritis are pain and stiffness in your joints, which can make it difficult to move the affected joints and do certain activities. The symptoms may come and go in episodes, which can be related to your activity levels and even the weather. In more severe cases, the symptoms can be continuous.

text_blocks.snippet: Arthritis is a condition characterized by inflammation and pain in one or more joints. It's not a single disease, but rather a term encompassing over 100 different conditions that affect joints and surrounding tissues.
snippet_highlighted_words: a condition characterized by inflammation and pain in one or more joints

text_blocks.snippet: Joints are the areas where two bones meet, like your elbows or knees. They allow for movement and flexibility.
Arthritis can be caused by a variety of factors, including:

list.snippet: Wear and tear: Osteoarthritis, the most common type, occurs when the cartilage that cushions the ends of bones wears down over time, causing bones to rub together.
Autoimmune diseases: In rheumatoid arthritis, the body's immune system mistakenly attacks the lining of the joints, causing inflammation and damage.
Infections: Bacteria or viruses can infect a joint, leading to inflammation and pain.
Injury: Joint injuries can sometimes lead to arthritis later in life.
Pain in one or more joints.
Stiffness, especially in the morning or after periods of inactivity.
Swelling and redness in the affected joint.
Decreased range of motion in the joint.
A feeling of warmth or heat in the joint.
Osteoarthritis: The most common type, often linked to aging and wear and tear.
Rheumatoid arthritis: An autoimmune disease that causes inflammation and damage to the joints.
Psoriatic arthritis: Affects some people with psoriasis, an autoimmune skin condition.
Gout: A painful condition caused by a buildup of uric acid in the joints.
Ankylosing spondylitis: Primarily affects the spine, causing inflammation, pain, and stiffness.
Septic arthritis: An infection in the joint, usually caused by bacteria or fungi.
